article_title: Federal and State Resources for Students Experiencing Homelessness
citation: Espinoza, D., Griffith, M., Burns, D., & Shields, P. M. (2023). Federal and state resources for students experiencing homelessness. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/546.264
title: McKinney-Vento Act framework of educational rights and district obligations for students experiencing homelessness
description: Title VII, subpart B, of the McKinney-Vento Homeless Assistance Act is the major federal framework establishing services and protections for students experiencing homelessness, requiring that they "have access to the same free, appropriate public education" as other children. It defines eligibility (lacking "a fixed, regular, and adequate nighttime residence") and obligates every LEA, funded or not, to designate a homeless liaison who identifies and enrolls students, ensures full participation, provides transportation, informs communities of rights, and refers families to housing, medical, dental, and mental health services.
requirements: Every LEA must designate a district homeless liaison, regardless of whether it receives McKinney-Vento funding
Liaisons must coordinate with state coordinators and community agencies providing education and related services
constraints: The report states the act is inadequately funded to accomplish its goals, and identification is challenged by stigma, housing instability, and limited district capacity
target_learners: Children and youths who lack a fixed, regular, and adequate nighttime residence
target_learning_goals: Equal access to free, appropriate public education
School stability and full participation
examples: LEA obligations include providing transportation to and from school regardless of where students are currently residing, and referring them to key resources such as housing and health services
key_sources: Espinoza, D., Griffith, M., Burns, D., & Shields, P. M. (2023). Federal and state resources for students experiencing homelessness. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/546.264

article_title: Learning Context: A Unified Framework and Roadmap for Context-Aware AI in Education
citation: Naiming Liu, Brittany Bradford, Johaun Hatchett, Gabriel Diaz, Lorenzo Luzi, Zichao Wang, Debshila Basu Mallick, Richard Baraniuk. (2025). Learning Context: A Unified Framework and Roadmap for Context-Aware AI in Education. https://www.openstax.org
title: Model Context Protocol (MCP) as the interoperability layer for warm-starting AI education tools
description: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is the open-standards mechanism the article proposes for making Learning Context portable across AI tools, so that learner context accumulated in one system can be consumed by another. "By leveraging the Model Context Protocol (MCP), we will enable a wide range of AI tools to “warm-start” with durable context and achieve continual, long-term personalization." MCP addresses the problem that context is lost whenever a learner switches tools, and is one of the four research questions of the LC technology theme: how modern AI systems can interoperate securely through open standards.
requirements: Standardized metadata ensuring cross-system consistency and interoperability across AI tools and learning platforms
constraints: Realizing cross-tool context portability requires substantial R&D on scalable, privacy-aware data infrastructure
target_learners: Learners who use multiple AI tools and learning platforms across their learning journeys
target_learning_goals: Continual, long-term personalization via durable, portable learner context
examples: The article's implementation strategy embeds the LC in the OpenStax digital learning platform ecosystem with SafeInsights privacy-preserving enclaves
key_sources: Naiming Liu, Brittany Bradford, Johaun Hatchett, Gabriel Diaz, Lorenzo Luzi, Zichao Wang, Debshila Basu Mallick, Richard Baraniuk. (2025). Learning Context: A Unified Framework and Roadmap for Context-Aware AI in Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24362

article_title: Mechanics Cognitive Diagnostic: Testing Fine-Grained Learning Objectives in Introductory Physics
citation: Vy Le, Jayson M. Nissen, Jason W. Morphew, Hua Hua Chang, and Ben Van Dusen. (2026). Mechanics Cognitive Diagnostic: Testing Fine-Grained Learning Objectives in Introductory Physics. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.09584
title: MCD-v2: a cognitive diagnostic computerized adaptive test reporting mastery of 14 fine-grained learning objectives in introductory mechanics
description: MCD-v2 is "a cognitive diagnostic computerized adaptive test that reports students' mastery of fine-grained learning objectives (LOs) throughout instruction." It was built with evidence-centered design: the authors "defined 14 LOs from introductory mechanics textbooks and AP Physics standards, mapped FCI, FMCE, and EMCS items onto them with a Q-matrix." Unlike fixed-length pretest-posttest RBAs, it is designed to be administered adaptively during a semester, giving instructors and students LO-level mastery feedback during instruction rather than after a course ends. The item bank reuses assessments physics courses already administer, delivered through the LASSO platform.
requirements: An item bank covering the targeted LOs with sufficient items per LO, and a validated Q-matrix connecting items to LOs
Response data large enough to stabilize DINA parameter estimates, gathered through the LASSO platform
constraints: The current bank covers only 14 of the 35 planned LOs and lacks items for rotational mechanics and mathematical reasoning
Establishing measurement invariance across administrations is required before interpreting change in LO mastery over time
target_learners: College students in introductory algebra-based and calculus-based mechanics courses
target_learning_goals: 14 mechanics learning objectives spanning vectors, kinematics, Newton's laws, energy, and momentum
key_sources: Vy Le, Jayson M. Nissen, Jason W. Morphew, Hua Hua Chang, and Ben Van Dusen. (2026). Mechanics Cognitive Diagnostic: Testing Fine-Grained Learning Objectives in Introductory Physics. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.09584

article_title: A study of the relationship between institutional policy, organisational culture and e-learning use in four South African universities
citation: Czerniewicz, L. & Brown, C. (2009). A study of the relationship between institutional policy, organisational culture and elearning use in four South African universities. Computers & Education, 53, 121-131. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2009.01.006
title: McNay's four-type organisational culture taxonomy combined with Structured/Unstructured elearning policy types as an analytic framework
description: The study frames institutional elearning contexts using two axes: an elearning policy typology (Structured versus Unstructured, defined by policy document, formal support unit and institution-wide LMS) and McNay's (1995) taxonomy of organisational cultures. The article describes the four cultural types: the collegium has "loose institutional policy definition, informal networks and decision arenas, and innovation at the level of the individual or department"; the bureaucracy has loose policy but strong regulation; the corporation has tight policy and tight implementation with top-down directives; the enterprise has a well-defined policy framework with students as clients. Institutions are classified by combining both axes.
requirements: Classification requires evidence on leadership style, institutional approach to ICT integration, and organisational style of policy implementation, drawn from key-informant interviews and prior research
constraints: The article notes no institution falls neatly into one grouping and institutions may change classification over time
The study does not cover all permutations; Structured Collegium and Structured Enterprise types were missing
target_learning_goals: understanding how institutional context shapes elearning adoption and use
examples: Four institutions were classified: A-S-Corp and B-S-Corp as Structured Corporations, C-U-Coll as Unstructured Collegium, D-U-Bur as Unstructured Bureaucracy
key_sources: Czerniewicz, L. & Brown, C. (2009). A study of the relationship between institutional policy, organisational culture and elearning use in four South African universities. Computers & Education, 53, 121-131. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2009.01.006

article_title: Simulation models in direct ophthalmoscopy education: a systematic review.
citation: Dutt Deepaysh DCS, Hohnen Harry, Kulshrestha Subham, Razavi Hessom. (2025). Simulation models in direct ophthalmoscopy education: a systematic review. Canadian Medical Education Journal. https://doi.org/10.36834/cmej.79989
title: McGaghie's levels of simulation-based translational outcomes as applied to direct ophthalmoscopy simulation
description: The review applies McGaghie's proposed levels of simulation-based translational outcomes, adapted to direct ophthalmoscopy, as an effectiveness assessment framework. Levels range from "Internal acceptability" (trainee satisfaction with simulator, Level 1) through "Contained effects" (changes in performance using the simulator, Level 2), "Downstream effects" (changes in clinical behaviour, Level 3), "Target effects" (changes in patient outcomes, Level 4) and "Collateral effects" (hospital-wide or systems-level changes, Level 5). The review uses this scale alongside the Kirkpatrick Model and a Messick-based validity scale to rate each included study.
requirements: Each study's simulator design is rated against the five translational outcome levels, from internal acceptability to collateral effects
constraints: The framework as applied assesses simulation effectiveness at levels up to system-wide change, but most included studies reached only Level 1 or 2
target_learning_goals: Direct ophthalmoscopy technique
Fundus pathology identification
examples: The review rated each of the 37 included studies' effectiveness using this adapted scale, reported in Appendix A
key_sources: Dutt Deepaysh DCS, Hohnen Harry, Kulshrestha Subham, Razavi Hessom. (2025). Simulation models in direct ophthalmoscopy education: a systematic review. Canadian Medical Education Journal. https://doi.org/10.36834/cmej.79989

article_title: Leadership and management competency frameworks in undergraduate medical education: a scoping review.
citation: Alhadithi Ahmed, Almansour Mohammed. (2025). Leadership and management competency frameworks in undergraduate medical education: a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08489-6
title: McKimm et al. three-level leadership framework (intrapersonal, interpersonal, organizational)
description: The review used the three-level leadership framework proposed by McKimm et al., also called the 'Swansea daffodil' model, as its analytical lens. It "categorizes MLM competencies into the following three levels: Intrapersonal: Self-awareness, personal attributes, and self-leadership. Interpersonal: Communication, teamwork, relationship building, and the ability to influence others. Organizational: Understanding and managing healthcare systems, leading change, and engaging in strategic leadership." The framework aligns with the developmental progression from 'leading self' to 'leading others' to 'leading systems'.
requirements: Competencies are coded by best-fit when plausibly fitting more than one domain, based on the dominant emphasis within the original publication
constraints: Selected for its structured, holistic lens aligned with the developmental progression of medical students
target_learning_goals: medical leadership and management competencies
key_sources: Alhadithi Ahmed, Almansour Mohammed. (2025). Leadership and management competency frameworks in undergraduate medical education: a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08489-6

article_title: Influence of Meta-Cognitive Training and Cognitive Styles on Numeracy Achievement of Nigerian Pupils' in Computer-Mediated Classrooms
citation: Taiwo Oladunni Gbenga-Akanmu & Philip Olu Jegede. (2019). Influence of Meta-cognitive Training and Cognitive Styles on Numeracy Achievement of Nigerian Pupils’ in Computer-mediated Classrooms. World Journal of Education, 9(1). https://doi.org/10.5430/wje.v9n1p221
title: Meta-cognitive Training Manual (MCTM) with the CRIME strategy acronym
description: The MCTM is the treatment instrument used to deliver meta-cognitive training to the experimental group. It was adapted from a model developed by Teong Su Kwang (2000) and "comprised the acronym (CRIME) Ca reful Reading, Re-call, Implement, Monitor and Evaluation of one's learning". The researchers used it to develop a lesson plan for the training, which taught pupils to think, recall, put into practice what has been taught, and apply it in new or similar situations.
requirements: Delivered as training sessions with class work reviewed by the researcher to ensure pupils followed the instructions
constraints: Adapted from a model originally developed for meta-cognitive training in mathematical word-problem solving (Teong, 2000)
target_learning_goals: metacognitive awareness and self-regulated answering of numeracy questions
examples: Training ran for 3 weeks, twice a week, with 30-minute sessions, using practical examples with real-life items
key_sources: Taiwo Oladunni Gbenga-Akanmu & Philip Olu Jegede. (2019). Influence of Meta-cognitive Training and Cognitive Styles on Numeracy Achievement of Nigerian Pupils’ in Computer-mediated Classrooms. World Journal of Education, 9(1). https://doi.org/10.5430/wje.v9n1p221

article_title: A Comparison of Heritage Learners and L2 Learners of Spanish: A Study on Compliment Sequences in the Classroom
citation: Bachelor, J. W., & Barros García, M. J. (2019). A comparison of heritage learners and L2 learners of Spanish: A study on compliment sequences in the classroom. Journal of Foreign Language Education and Technology, 4(1). http://jflet.com/jflet/
title: Multiple-Choice Discourse Completion Test (MCDCT) for Spanish compliment sequences
description: An original instrument designed by the researchers to assess recognition of compliments and compliment responses in Spanish. It "consisted of ten questions, five compliments and five compliment responses; of those, five were formal situations, and five were informal situations," with students choosing the most appropriate response for each scenario. Correct answers were real responses provided by ten native Spanish speakers, selected to reflect research on Spanish compliment strategies.
requirements: Correct answers must reflect pragmatic norms evidenced in prior research on Spanish compliment responses
Scenarios must present a situation with multiple-choice response options
constraints: The researchers recognize that students are only being assessed on recognition rather than on pragmatic production
There is some debate even among native speakers as to which answer is the correct answer on these types of instruments
target_learning_goals: pragmatic recognition of Spanish compliments and compliment responses
examples: Used as both pretest and posttest for all 62 participants across the four groups during the 2017-2018 academic year
key_sources: Bachelor, J. W., & Barros García, M. J. (2019). A comparison of heritage learners and L2 learners of Spanish: A study on compliment sequences in the classroom. Journal of Foreign Language Education and Technology, 4(1). http://jflet.com/jflet/

article_title: Measuring Effectiveness of Information, Communication and Technology (ICT) Tools in Teaching School Children: A Case Study from Chattisgarh State, India
citation: J. Durga Prasad Rao & Raksha Singh. (2011). Measuring effectiveness of Information, Communication and Technology (ICT) tools in teaching school children: A case study from Chattisgarh state, India. i-manager's Journal of School Educational Technology, 6(3).
title: Multiple-choice achievement test on three primary-curriculum topics used as pre-test and post-test
description: The study's outcome measure was an achievement test of multiple-choice questions with four options covering three topics drawn from the primary school curriculum: Various Modes of Transportation, basic pollution causes, and Tips for healthy living. It was administered before and after teaching, with a three-hour interval between pre-test and post-test, and gain scores were computed for each pupil. The DLP clips on the three topics were produced locally and edited for suitability, taking the children's socio-cultural status into consideration.
requirements: Topics drawn from the primary school curriculum; DLP clips produced locally and edited for suitability for teaching children
constraints: A three-hour interval was given between pre-test and post-test
target_learners: Primary and secondary school pupils in Chhattisgarh, India
target_learning_goals: Achievement on curriculum topics: modes of transportation, pollution causes, healthy living
examples: 100 pupils stratified along primary and secondary class in three schools were placed 25 per treatment group and tested before and after instruction
key_sources: J. Durga Prasad Rao & Raksha Singh. (2011). Measuring effectiveness of Information, Communication and Technology (ICT) tools in teaching school children: A case study from Chattisgarh state, India. i-manager's Journal of School Educational Technology, 6(3). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1102746

article_title: Alleviating Mathematics Anxiety of Elementary School Students: A Situated Perspective
citation: Sharma, Y. (2016). Alleviating mathematics anxiety of elementary school students: A situated perspective. International Journal of Research in Education and Science (IJRES), 2(2), 509-517. https://www.ijres.net
title: McLellan's situated learning model with eight key components
description: The study applies McLellan's (1991, 1996) situated learning model, the instructional application of situated cognition theory, in which knowledge is co-constructed socially rather than transmitted as abstract, decontextualised content. The article states that "The key components of the situated learning model are stories, reflection, cognitive apprenticeship, collaboration, coaching, multiple practices, articulation of learning skills and technology." In this study these eight components structured the mathematics lessons used as the experimental treatment.
requirements: Lessons must be developed around the model's eight key components, as the study did for grade VII mathematics
constraints: The article notes McLellan (1996) held that "a great deal of work is needed to fine -tune theory and assess how to tran sform theory into practice"
target_learning_goals: alleviating mathematics anxiety while learning grade VII mathematics
examples: Grade VII mathematics lessons were built on the components: video tutorials for technology, Polya's problem solving model for articulation of learning skills, Jigsaw II for collaboration, and a synthesis of Van Hiele's theory with cognitive apprenticeship
key_sources: Sharma, Y. (2016). Alleviating mathematics anxiety of elementary school students: A situated perspective. International Journal of Research in Education and Science (IJRES), 2(2), 509-517. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1110268

article_title: Effect of Blended Learning Educational Model on Secondary School Students' Mathematics Conceptual Understanding
citation: Abdissa, D. G., Duressa, G. F., Olkaba, T. T., & Feyissa, E. G. (2024). Effect of blended learning educational model on secondary school students' mathematics conceptual understanding. Problems of Education in the 21st Century, 82(5), 585–599. https://doi.org/10.33225/pec/24.82.585
title: Mathematics Conceptual Understanding Test (MCUT): an 18-item two-tier multiple-choice diagnostic instrument
description: The MCUT is a researcher-developed diagnostic test of grade-10 mathematics conceptual understanding covering relations and functions, polynomial functions, and exponential and logarithmic functions. It uses a two-tier format in which "the first tier involves answering content-related questions, while the second tier includes multiple-choice questions and a blank space for further explanation." Items are scored 0–3 on a right-answer/right-reason rubric, with total scores ranging from 0 to 100. Reliability and item statistics were checked after piloting.
requirements: Pilot testing and validity/reliability checking via the KR-20 coefficient, discrimination index, and mean difficulty level before use
constraints: Reliability was acceptable but moderate: KR-20 = 0.72, discrimination index .39, mean difficulty .36, as printed by the article
target_learning_goals: Conceptual understanding of relations and functions, polynomial, exponential, and logarithmic functions
examples: Administered as identical pre-test and post-test to both groups over a 20-week intervention from September 2023 to February 2024
key_sources: Abdissa, D. G., Duressa, G. F., Olkaba, T. T., & Feyissa, E. G. (2024). Effect of blended learning educational model on secondary school students' mathematics conceptual understanding. Problems of Education in the 21st Century, 82(5), 585–599. https://doi.org/10.33225/pec/24.82.585

article_title: Teaching Formulaic Sequences in an English-Language Class: The Effects of Explicit Instruction versus Coursebook Instruction
citation: Le-Thi, D., Rodgers, M. P. H., & Pellicer-Sánchez, A. (2017). Teaching Formulaic Sequences in an English-Language Class: The Effects of Explicit Instruction Versus Coursebook Instruction. TESL Canada Journal/Revue TESL du Canada, 34(3), 111–139. http://dx.doi.org/10.18806/tesl.v34i3.1276
title: Two multiple-choice tests (cloze and translation) for measuring receptive knowledge of form and meaning of formulaic sequences.
description: The study created two multiple-choice tests to measure learners' knowledge of 69 formulaic sequences: a cloze test measuring "learners' ability to recognize receptive knowledge of form and meaning of the sequences presented in sentence contexts" and a translation test measuring "form and meaning recognition of the target items without context." Distractors were created using the Nagy, Anderson, and Herman (1987) procedure at three levels of difficulty, with six options per item (correct answer plus five distractors). Dichotomous scoring was used, and the tests served as pretests, posttests, and delayed posttests.
requirements: Distractors designed at different levels of difficulty following the Nagy, Anderson, and Herman (1987) procedure
Test items presented in a different order for each test administration to control for order effects
constraints: Tests measured only receptive knowledge of form and meaning; the authors note future research should consider tests measuring other aspects of formulaic sequence knowledge
target_learning_goals: Receptive knowledge of form and meaning of formulaic sequences
examples: Cloze test example: 'People join groups for ___ motivation, learning, and support.' with correct answer 'all sorts of' and five distractors including 'on average' and 'find out'

article_title: Effects of Interim Assessments on the Achievement Gap: Evidence from an Experiment
citation: Konstantopoulos, S., Li, W., Miller, S., & van der Ploeg, A. (2015). Effects of Interim Assessments on the Achievement Gap: Evidence from an Experiment. SREE Spring 2015 Conference. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED555398
title: mCLASS and Acuity interim assessment programs
description: The study evaluated two interim assessment programs administered multiple times per school year. In grades K-2, mCLASS diagnostic probes are conducted face-to-face; for reading and ELA, "the student performs language tasks while the teacher records characteristics of the work using a personal digital assistant (PDA)," while mCLASS mathematics uses paper and pencil with results entered by the teacher. CTB/McGraw-Hill's Acuity provides online assessments in reading and mathematics for grades 3-8, consisting of 30- to 35-item multiple-choice online tests aligned to Indiana standards.
requirements: Schools received the assessment programs along with training associated with each program
constraints: Assessments are closely aligned to Indiana standards and also aligned to some degree to the Indiana state test
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement
reading achievement
examples: In the experiment, treatment schools received mCLASS and Acuity with associated training, while control schools operated under business-as-usual conditions
key_sources: Konstantopoulos, S., Li, W., Miller, S., & van der Ploeg, A. (2015). Effects of Interim Assessments on the Achievement Gap: Evidence from an Experiment. SREE Spring 2015 Conference. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED562166

article_title: Implementing team-based sequential simulation for medical students in clinical clerkship: preliminary findings and learning efficiency evaluation.
citation: Liu Hsin-Liang, Lu Peih-Ying, Hsu Anna Shan-Chun, Lin Yen-Ko, Chan Kwong D., Lee Chien-Hsing, Chang Po-Chih. (2026). Implementing team-based sequential simulation for medical students in clinical clerkship: preliminary findings and learning efficiency evaluation. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09412-3
title: mCLEIMS station design: six teams rotating through six 25-minute sequential simulation stations
description: The 2-day mCLEIMS course organized 108 students into six teams of six per session, rotating through six specialty stations (pediatrics, traumatology, internal medicine, geriatrics, obstetrics/gynecology, emergency medicine). "Each station lasted 25 min: 2 min of facilitator briefing, 18 min of team task performance, 1 min of team-leader summary, and 4 min of reflection and feedback." Stations were linked as a patient journey rather than isolated exercises.
requirements: Preparatory information and learning objectives provided in a pre-brief at the start of each session
constraints: Condensed 2-day format adapted because of local curricular requirements, scheduling constraints, and limited resources
target_learning_goals: clinical skills
interprofessional collaboration
communication
patient safety
examples: Students rotated through stations covering progressive phases of care including first contact, assessment, deterioration, handoff, and discharge planning
key_sources: Liu Hsin-Liang, Lu Peih-Ying, Hsu Anna Shan-Chun, Lin Yen-Ko, Chan Kwong D., Lee Chien-Hsing, Chang Po-Chih. (2026). BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09412-3

article_title: Pedagogical impact of different levels of e-learning teaching during anesthesia residency: a randomized clinical trial.
citation: Jean S, Thill J, Burey J, Besnier E, Lambert M, Lefevre-Scelles A, Abily J, Gastaldi G, Allard E, Hanouz J-L, Veber B, Dureuil B, Thill C, Compère V. (2026). Pedagogical impact of different levels of e-learning teaching during anesthesia residency: a randomized clinical trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09225-4
title: Gate module progression with MCQ validation to encourage regular work
description: The article's platform required residents to "validate at least a series of 4 multiple-choice questions (MCQs) on 5" before advancing to the next module, which the authors describe as similar to continuous assessment, "encouraging learners to work regularly". This gating mechanism structures self-paced study and prompts re-study when performance falls below the threshold.
requirements: A platform with sequential learning modules and scored MCQ assessments per module
constraints: In the trial, 7 of 28 residents (25%) considered validating the MCQs "difficult"
target_learning_goals: theoretical clinical knowledge
self-regulated study habits
examples: The Int-EL platform divided perioperative diabetic management into three modules, each gated by a 4-of-5 MCQ validation

article_title: Preliminary insights on high-fidelity embalming solutions for surgical skills training-An evaluation using the McMaster Embalming Scale and mechanical tests.
citation: Darie S., Wainman B.C., Wohl G.R., Wang A.Y., Zhang B.Z., Li A., Ahmad E., Palombella A.S., Rockarts J.L., de SA D.L., Nguyen L.N., DeCarlo B., Downer N., Brewer‐Deluce D. (2026). Preliminary insights on high‐fidelity embalming solutions for surgical skills training—An evaluation using the McMaster Embalming Scale and mechanical tests. Anatomical Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1002/ase.70185
title: McMaster Embalming Scale (MES)
description: The McMaster Embalming Scale (MES) is a validated qualitative instrument for systematically comparing differently embalmed tissues in surgical skills training contexts, assessing visual and tactile characteristics. "The scale consists of seven domains: decay, odor, color, visual appearance, texture, force, and suitability." Decay and odor, when present, are tracked on a 3-point Likert scale, while the five skill-dependent domains each use a 5-point Likert scale. It was created via a pilot study in 2022 and validated and generalized by Wang et al. using standardized porcine models, and in this study was completed by surgical residents at each testing station.
requirements: Trained raters familiar with the surgical skill being performed, with standardized instructions read to participants before scale administration
constraints: Ratings may be influenced by rater experience level, as less experienced participants may report more neutral ratings
target_learners: surgical residents evaluating embalmed donor tissue fidelity
target_learning_goals: evaluating tissue fidelity of embalmed donors for surgical skills training
examples: Used in a fully crossed double-blind study in which 23 surgical residents each performed three skills on four donors and completed the MES at 12 stations
key_sources: Darie S., Wainman B.C., Wohl G.R., Wang A.Y., Zhang B.Z., Li A., Ahmad E., Palombella A.S., Rockarts J.L., de SA D.L., Nguyen L.N., DeCarlo B., Downer N., Brewer‐Deluce D. (2026). Preliminary insights on high‐fidelity embalming solutions for surgical skills training—An evaluation using the McMaster Embalming Scale and mechanical tests. Anatomical Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1002/ase.70185

article_title: Evaluation of a Problem-Based Learning Program's Effect on Artificial Intelligence Ethics Among Japanese Medical Students: Mixed Methods Study.
citation: Chartash David, Bievre Nicolas, Marušić Ana, Ota Yuma, Asada Yoshikazu, Kubo Saori, Kanno Takeshi, Yagi Machiko Saeki, Matsuyama Yasushi. (2026). Evaluation of a Problem-Based Learning Program’s Effect on Artificial Intelligence Ethics Among Japanese Medical Students: Mixed Methods Study. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/84535
title: Use assessment measures beyond MCQs when evaluating PBL's higher-order skill outcomes
description: The article argues that standardized multiple-choice tests cannot adequately capture the higher-order abilities PBL fosters, such as clinical reasoning, metacognition, and communication. Although "MCQs are suitable to measure objective knowledge, they may have low sensitivity in capturing changes in the higher-order practical skills fostered by PBL." The study therefore supplemented MCQs with descriptive essays analyzed by text mining, which revealed the qualitative structural transformation in thinking that the MCQ gains did not. The authors call for developing and validating new assessment measures for practical reasoning and communication skills.
requirements: Complementary qualitative or performance-based measures (e.g., descriptive essays analyzed with text mining) alongside knowledge tests
constraints: The null additional PBL effect on MCQ scores does not by itself demonstrate higher-order learning; the qualitative interpretation is the authors' argument, and the study lacked a control group
target_learners: undergraduate medical students in PBL curricula
target_learning_goals: clinical reasoning and communication about AI ethics
metacognitive and higher-order thinking skills
examples: The study administered two descriptive essay questions at pretest and posttest and analyzed them with word-frequency, transition, and cooccurrence network analyses
key_sources: Chartash David, Bievre Nicolas, Marušić Ana, Ota Yuma, Asada Yoshikazu, Kubo Saori, Kanno Takeshi, Yagi Machiko Saeki, Matsuyama Yasushi. (2026). Evaluation of a Problem-Based Learning Program’s Effect on Artificial Intelligence Ethics Among Japanese Medical Students: Mixed Methods Study. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/84535

article_title: An Open-Source, AI-Supported Teaching Tool in Orthodontic Education-Assessment of Acceptance and Effectiveness.
citation: H. Sabbagh, T. Ribnishki, L. Hötzel, L. von Bronk, Y. Khazaei, and A. Wichelhaus. (2025). An Open‐Source, AI‐Supported Teaching Tool in Orthodontic Education—Assessment of Acceptance and Effectiveness. Journal of Dental Education 89(12): 1753–1764. https://doi.org/10.1002/jdd.13916
title: MCAT: an open-source AI-supported application for self-paced cephalometric tracing practice with automated feedback
description: MCAT (Munich Cephalometric Application for Training) is an open-source Python application, built on a pre-trained convolutional neural network for landmark recognition, through which "students had the opportunity to manually trace 16 cephalometric reference points on a lateral cephalometric image and compare their position with the points predicted by the pre-trained model". It provides ten training cephalograms across five dentoskeletal anomaly types, visual side-by-side display of student versus model points, and a quantitative diagram of absolute x/y deviations. It runs on students' personal computers, supporting location-independent, self-paced training, and was released via Open Data LMU.
requirements: Runs on students' personal computers with compatibility across common operating systems; includes teaching materials, a tracing tool, and an evaluation questionnaire in the interface.
constraints: The underlying pre-trained model achieved 84.73% landmark detection at 2 mm and 96.58% at 4 mm range, so a student's correct annotation risks being classified as deviant; the article states visual representation lets students check landmarks independently.
target_learners: Final-year undergraduate dental students in orthodontic education
target_learning_goals: Accurate identification of cephalometric anatomical landmarks and cephalometric analysis for malocclusion diagnosis and treatment planning
examples: In the pilot, intervention-semester students received a 2-h on-site training session guided by orthodontic residents and a senior orthodontist, then accessed MCAT remotely for 2 weeks before submitting three manually traced radiographs.
key_sources: H. Sabbagh, T. Ribnishki, L. Hötzel, L. von Bronk, Y. Khazaei, and A. Wichelhaus. (2025). An Open‐Source, AI‐Supported Teaching Tool in Orthodontic Education—Assessment of Acceptance and Effectiveness. Journal of Dental Education 89(12): 1753–1764. https://doi.org/10.1002/jdd.13916

article_title: Multi-source feedback in undergraduate medical education: a pilot study.
citation: Bartman I, St-Onge C, Roy M, Gingerich A, Katsoulas E, Chahine S, Gagnon N. (2025). Multi-source feedback in undergraduate medical education: a pilot study. Canadian Medical Education Journal. https://doi.org/10.36834/cmej.79283
title: MCC 360 UGME: an adapted multisource feedback tool for clerkship students with patient, self, and mixed rater groups and facilitated report review
description: The MCC 360 UGME is a multisource feedback tool adapted from the practising-physician MCC 360 for third-year clerkship students. It collects feedback from three rater groups — patients, self, and a mixed group of supervisors, residents, hospital staff and/or peers — compiles it into an individualized report, and pairs the report with an independent facilitator review session. The article reports that the tool 'incorporated MSF from three rater groups (patients, self, and a mixed group of supervisors, residents, hospital staff and/or peers) and compiled it into an individualized report.' Unlike prior UGME MSF uses, it includes the patient perspective, narrative feedback, and facilitated review.
requirements: Requires trained facilitators who have no influence over the clerk's promotion
Requires raters (patients, peers, supervisors, hospital staff) willing to complete surveys
Narrative comments must be screened to remove derogatory or offensive content before students see reports
constraints: Surveys are the intellectual property of the Medical Council of Canada and cannot be shared
Some clinical sites had too few students and supervisors to allow sufficient anonymity
target_learners: third-year clerkship medical students in undergraduate medical education programs
target_learning_goals: communication, collaboration, and professionalism competencies
feedback acceptance and reflective habits
examples: Piloted at one Canadian medical school in 2021 with eleven students, seven of whom completed the post-evaluation survey
key_sources: Bartman I, St-Onge C, Roy M, Gingerich A, Katsoulas E, Chahine S, Gagnon N. (2025). Multi-source feedback in undergraduate medical education: a pilot study. Canadian Medical Education Journal. https://doi.org/10.36834/cmej.79283

article_title: An evidence-based approach to understanding the competency development needs of the health service management workforce in Australia.
citation: Liang Zhanming, Blackstock Felicity C., Howard Peter F, Briggs David S, Leggat Sandra G, Wollersheim Dennis, Edvardsson David, Rahman Aziz. (2018). An evidence-based approach to understanding the competency development needs of the health service management workforce in Australia. BMC Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-018-3760-z
title: MCAP Leadership and Management Competency Framework: six core management competencies measured by 79 behavioural items
description: The MCAP Leadership and Management Competency Framework is a competency framework purpose-built for healthcare settings and health service manager assessment. It was developed through a staged process adapting prior frameworks, and "consisting of the following six core management competencies that are measured by 79 behavioural items": evidence-informed decision-making; operations, administration and resource management; knowledge of healthcare environment and the organisation; interpersonal communication and relationship management; leading people and organisations; and enabling and managing change. Competence is rated on a 7-point behavioural scale from not competent to superior expertise.
requirements: Assessment via the MCAP 360° tool involving self, supervisor, peer and report raters
A 7-point behavioural scale on which a score of five or more defines competence
constraints: Purpose built for the healthcare setting and HSM competency assessment
Developed and validated in Victoria, Australia
target_learners: Middle-level health service managers in public hospitals and community health services
target_learning_goals: Managerial competency development in evidence-informed decision-making, resource management, healthcare environment knowledge, communication, leadership and change management
examples: The study applied the framework to 93 middle-level managers from two public hospitals and five community health services between 2012 and 2014
key_sources: Liang Zhanming, Blackstock Felicity C., Howard Peter F, Briggs David S, Leggat Sandra G, Wollersheim Dennis, Edvardsson David, Rahman Aziz. (2018). An evidence-based approach to understanding the competency development needs of the health service management workforce in Australia. BMC Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-018-3760-z

article_title: An evidence-based approach to understanding the competency development needs of the health service management workforce in Australia.
citation: Liang Zhanming, Blackstock Felicity C., Howard Peter F, Briggs David S, Leggat Sandra G, Wollersheim Dennis, Edvardsson David, Rahman Aziz. (2018). An evidence-based approach to understanding the competency development needs of the health service management workforce in Australia. BMC Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-018-3760-z
title: MCAP Tool: online 360° management competency assessment tool
description: The MCAP Tool is an online evidence-based management competency assessment tool comprising a 360° assessment involving self, supervisor, colleague and supervisee raters. It was developed and validated in Victoria between 2012 and 2014, hosted on a web-based platform built by the research team, and administers the 79 behavioural items covering the six MCAP competencies on a 7-point Likert scale. The article reports it "is a reliable and valid measure of HSM managerial competency" and demonstrates its use for identifying individual behavioural items requiring improvement for targeted professional development.
requirements: Completion by the manager (self) plus supervisor, peer and report raters
A web-based platform for hosting and analysing assessments
constraints: Subjective assessment only; the article notes measurement of performance as a quantitative outcome is needed to confirm the relationship with assessed competency
target_learning_goals: Identification of individual managerial competency gaps for targeted professional development
examples: In the study, 93 managers and 319 colleagues completed the tool, with a near 100% completion rate for the 79 behavioural items and only 3% missing data points
key_sources: Liang Zhanming, Blackstock Felicity C., Howard Peter F, Briggs David S, Leggat Sandra G, Wollersheim Dennis, Edvardsson David, Rahman Aziz. (2018). An evidence-based approach to understanding the competency development needs of the health service management workforce in Australia. BMC Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-018-3760-z

article_title: Unpacking the "Black Box": How an SMS-Based Continuing Medical Education Intervention Improved Medical Knowledge Among HIV Clinicians in Vietnam.
citation: Nofal MR, Halim N, Le BN, et al. (2018). Unpacking the “black box”: how an SMS-based continuing medical education intervention improved medical knowledge among HIV clinicians in Vietnam. Glob Health Sci Pract. 2018;6(4):668-679. https://doi.org/10.9745/GHSP-D-18-00298
title: mCME version 2.0 intervention: daily SMS quizzes, hyperlinked daily readings, and online CME courses for HIV clinicians in Vietnam
description: mCME version 2.0 was a 6-month mobile continuing medical education intervention conducted between 2016 and 2017 with 106 HIV clinicians (53 intervention, 53 control). The intervention group received “an SMS with a multiple choice question once daily along with a reply congratulating for correct answers or encouraging better luck next time while providing the correct answer,” plus a daily hyperlink to technical readings typically 13 paragraphs long and invitations to online CME courses hosted by Hanoi Medical University. Content was clustered thematically into 15 modules covering clinical HIV/AIDS care; quizzes were developed in English and translated into Vietnamese, with other components delivered in Vietnamese.
requirements: Participants must own a smartphone and have access to a mobile network
Software and broadcast content must be made available by the supporting groups
constraints: The control group received only weekly non-medical reminder SMS messages; both groups had baseline access to the online CME courses
target_learners: HIV clinicians in Vietnam, including community-based physician's assistants and physicians
target_learning_goals: Medical knowledge across 15 clinical HIV/AIDS care topic areas
examples: Among intervention participants, on average 82% of daily quizzes were answered and about half answered correctly; only 18.1% of daily hyperlinks were accessed on average
key_sources: Nofal MR, Halim N, Le BN, et al. (2018). Unpacking the “black box”: how an SMS-based continuing medical education intervention improved medical knowledge among HIV clinicians in Vietnam. Glob Health Sci Pract. 2018;6(4):668-679. https://doi.org/10.9745/GHSP-D-18-00298

article_title: Effectiveness of PBL methodology in a hybrid dentistry program to enhance students' knowledge and confidence. (a pilot study).
citation: Al-Madi Ebtissam M, Celur Sree Lalita, Nasim Mamoona. (2018). Effectiveness of PBL methodology in a hybrid dentistry program to enhance students’ knowledge and confidence. (a pilot study). BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-018-1392-y
title: Paper-based assessment tool pairing 30 single-best-answer MCQs with 5-point confidence items
description: A paper-based instrument combining knowledge and confidence measurement: it comprises "30 multiple choice questions (MCQs) of the single best type", 15 built from didactic-lecture topics and 15 from PBL topics, each scored 0 or 1. Every MCQ is followed by a confidence item on a 5-point Likert scale ranging from "0 = not sure at all" to "4 = extremely sure". The tool was checked for construct validity and administered identically at pre-course, post-course, and pre-clinics time points.
requirements: The same instrument must be reused across all evaluation time points to allow paired comparison of knowledge and confidence scores.
constraints: The authors list as a limitation that the study used only MCQs to assess student knowledge.
target_learning_goals: Head and Neck Anatomy knowledge
self-reported confidence in answering knowledge questions
examples: Administered to 33 first-year students before the course, immediately after it, and 15 months later before clinical courses.
key_sources: Al-Madi Ebtissam M, Celur Sree Lalita, Nasim Mamoona. (2018). Effectiveness of PBL methodology in a hybrid dentistry program to enhance students’ knowledge and confidence. (a pilot study). BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-018-1392-y
